analytic.title: Schedulability Analysis for Messages in Gateway-Interconnected Controller Area Network

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Controller Area Network (CAN) is widely used inside the automobiles. To decrease design complexity and cost, several CAN are utilized in different sub systems and gateway is employed to realize the communication between them. But the employment of gateway brings many challenges for schedulability analysis of CAN messages. We first analyzed the key challenges for schedulability analysis of messages. And then, based on existing method proposed for one single CAN, a new analysis method that is based on interference analysis for dynamically arriving gateway messages is proposed for nongateway messages. Furthermore, a division approach that transforms the end-to-end schedulability analysis of gateway messages into the similar situation with that of non-gateway messages is proposed for gateway messages. The proposed method is proved to be safe, and by comparing it with a full space searching based simulator and applying to a real message set, its effectiveness is demonstrated as well.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: To meet the requirements from safety, energy efficiency and infotainment, more and more sensors, actuators and ECUs are added into the automobiles, which increased the complexity of the automotive networks to a large extent [1]. CAN is currently the most widely used network technology inside the automotive electronic system. To reduce design complexity and cost, several CAN are utilized in different sub systems, such as the body system, powertrain system and information system. Therefore, gateway is employed to enable the communication between different CAN [1,2]. The basic function of gateway is to realize the message exchange between different CAN, where messages from one CAN are first stored in queue inside the gateway and then forwarded into another CAN when they win the arbitration. But other complex functions such as jitter reduction and message filtering, which can reduce the worst-case response time (WCRT) for messages and the bus load for CAN can also be implemented inside the gateway [3,4].

As automotive electronic system is generally a hard real time system, we must guarantee the real-time capability of CAN messages, or else it will result in a catastrophic situation. Thus, schedulability analysis is a must for CAN messages. Although message's schedulability analysis for one single CAN has attracted much attention since 1994 [5,6], the adding of gateway brings many new challenges, thus the existing methods proposed for one single CAN cannot be reused. There are very few related works about the gatewayinterconnected CAN: Sommer and Andblind [3] proposed a CAN-CAN gateway embedded system, where the resource dimensioning problems such as the gateway processing time and buffer capacity are investigated; Davis and Navet [4] proposed a method to reduce the jitter for gateway messages; Sojka et al. [7] proposed a measurement based method to analyze the latency introduced by gateway. However, no message's schedulability analysis method is proposed in these works. Although there are industry tools claiming to support message's WCRT analysis for gatewayinterconnected CAN, their methods are confidential. To the best of our knowledge, there is no such publication that gives a schedulability analysis method for messages in gatewayinterconnected CAN.

The main contributions of this work are as follows: first, it analyzed the main challenges for schedulability analysis of messages in gateway-interconnected CAN; and then it proposed a method to tackle such challenges and can get the safe upper bound of the WCRT for messages, the safety of the proposed method is proved and the effectiveness of it is demonstrated as well. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: section II gives the system model and assumptions, section III presents the problem analysis, section IV gives the interference analysis for dynamically arriving gateway messages, and then the concrete WCRT analysis method is proposed in section V, section VI shows the experimental results and this paper is concluded in section VII.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL AND ASSUMPTIONS
div.p: We assume that automotive electronic system consists of two sub systems as shown in Fig. 1, and each sub system includes several ECUs that are connected by CAN. The included two CAN have the same bandwidth and are interconnected by gateway, where messages are exchanged to realize the communication between two sub systems. Each ECU ECU N includes a message set S N that needs to be transmitted on CAN. As the priority is unique for each message, we use the symbol m i with the subscript indicating Figure 1. System architecture for automotive electronic system its priority to represent it. Thus, S N = {m i |m i ∈ S N }. m i is indicated by a 4-tuple: < T i , P i , C i , D i >, which represent the period, priority, transmission time and deadline, respectively, and we assume that T i =D i . If i < j, it means that m i has higher priority than m j . For two communicating ECUs that belong to the same sub system, the communicating messages will be only transmitted on the included CAN of the corresponding sub system, we define this kind of message as non-gateway message and the included CAN as its source CAN CAN sou . Such as m 2 in ECU 1 is a nongateway message and its CAN sou is CAN 1 . For two communicating ECUs that belong to different sub systems, the communicating messages will be transmitted on its CAN sou first, and then go through the gateway and be transmitted on the other CAN again, we define this kind of message as gateway message and the other CAN as its destination CAN CAN des . Such as m 1 in ECU 1 is a gateway message, its CAN sou is CAN 1 and its CAN des is CAN 2 . For non-gateway message, to keep the consistency of the notation with that of the gateway message, the other CAN is also defined as its destination CAN CAN des , for example CAN 2 is the CAN des of m 2 .

As this paper mostly focus on the analysis of message's response time, the following assumptions are made about the gateway to simplify the analysis [3]: in each transmission direction for example from CAN 1 to CAN 2 , there is a set of queues (include the input and output queue) to realize the store and forward operation for message exchange, hence the messages from different transmission directions will not interfere with each other inside the gateway; messages are managed with the fixed-priority based policy inside the queues, and we ignore the processing time inside the gateway for gateway messages.

div.head: III. PROBLEM ANALYSIS
div.p: For the following parts, we always assume that the object message for schedulability analysis is m i . We define the WCRT of m i as the maximal interval between the release time in its host ECU and the finish time in its destination ECU. However, as the transmission path for non-gateway and gateway message are different, we have to differentiate the WCRT for these two kinds of messages. If m i is a nongateway message, it will be transmitted on its CAN sou only, thus we indicate its WCRT as r s,i . But if m i is a gateway message, the transmission path will includes its CAN sou , gateway and its CAN des , the corresponding WCRT is usually called end-to-end WCRT, thus we indicate it as r e2e,i . For message's WCRT analysis, the key is to analyze all the possible interference that would happen to it, thus next we will focus on interference analysis for m i . If m i is a nongateway message, four different types of messages will interfere with m i as shown in Fig. 2(a). shp(i) and slp(i) represent two sets of messages that come from m i 's CAN sou and have higher and lower priority than m i , respectively. dhp GW (i) and dlp GW (i) represent the other two sets of messages that come from m i 's CAN des and have higher and lower priority than m i , respectively. The subscript GW indicates the message set is a gateway message set. dhp GW (i) is only a sub set of dhp(i), dhp(i) also includes the other nongateway messages. For example for m 2 in Fig. 1, shp(2)= {m 1 }, slp(2)={m 3 , m 4 , m 8 }, dhp GW (2) ={}, dlp GW (2)={m 5 , m 6 }. The interference pattern of shp(i) messages is periodic as they belong to the same CAN with m i , thus we can reuse the existing method proposed for one single CAN to analyze their interference [6]. slp(i) and dlp GW (i) messages can cause the priority inversion to m i only once, therefore we can include their interference by choosing the message with the maximal C k [6]. But for dhp GW (i) messages, they need to be scheduled in m i 's CAN des first, and then arrive at m i 's CAN sou and cause interference on m i . The finishing time in m i 's CAN des is equals to its arriving time in m i 's CAN sou for dhp GW (i) messages because of the ignoring of processing time inside the gateway. And as the response time for each instance of dhp GW (i) messages in m i 's CAN des are different, the arriving pattern of dhp GW (i) messages in m i 's CAN sou is dynamic. Thus, how to define the interference from the dynamic arriving dhp GW (i) messages is a challenge for r s,i 's analysis. Furthermore, as shown in Fig. 1, gateway messages from CAN 1 such as m 1 , m 3 and m 4 will interfere with messages that belong to CAN 2 , and conversely gateway messages from CAN 2 such as m 5 and m 6 will also interfere with messages that belong to CAN 1 . Consequently, another challenge for r s,i 's analysis that is also brought by gateway messages is the inter-dependency between messages in two CAN.

If m i is a gateway message, the complexity for r e2e,i 's analysis will be much bigger compared with that of r s,i , because we need to analyze the interference that would happen to m i in two CAN. When m i is transmitted on its CAN sou , all the possible kinds of interfering messages are the same with that of r s,i 's analysis for non-gateway messages. When m i is transmitted on its CAN des , another three types of messages will interfere with m i as shown in Fig. 2(b). dhp(i) and dlp(i) represent two sets of messages that belong to m i 's CAN des and have higher or lower priority than m i , respectively. shp GW (i) represents the set of gateway messages that belongs to m i 's CAN sou and has higher priority than m i . As CAN messages are scheduled non-preemptively, slp GW (i) messages cannot arrive at m i 's CAN des at the same time with m i , hence it cannot cause the priority inversion to m i . Take m 3 for example, when in its
div.formula: CAN sou , shp(3)={m 1 , m 2 }, slp(3)= {m 4 , m 8 }, dhp GW (3)={}, dlp GW (3)={m 5 , m 6 }; when in its CAN des , shp GW (3)={m 1 }, dhp(3)={}, dlp(3)={m 5 , m 6 , m 7 }.
div.p: For dlp GW (i) and slp(i) messages when m i in its CAN sou and for dlp(i) messages when m i in its CAN des , as they can cause priority inversion to m i only once, we can easily include their interference by choosing the message with the maximal C k , respectively. When m i in its CAN sou , the interference pattern of shp(i) messages is periodic, but part of shp(i) messages are also gateway messages as well, which are the shp GW (i) messages when m i in its CAN des , and their interference pattern is changed to be dynamic. Thus first, the interference pattern is changeable from periodic to dynamic in two CAN for shp GW (i) messages; and furthermore, the interference caused by shp GW (i) messages is inter-dependent in two CAN. The same situation also happens to dhp(i) messages when m i in its CAN des . Take m 6 for example, when m 6 in its CAN sou CAN 2 , m 5 belongs to shp(i) and its interference pattern is periodic, m 1 belongs to dhp GW (i) and its interference pattern is dynamic; but after m 6 going through the gateway and arriving at its CAN des CAN 1 , m 5 belongs to shp GW (i) and its interference pattern is changed to be dynamic, m 1 belongs to dhp(i) and its interference pattern is changed to be periodic. Consequently first, the challenges that are met for r s,i 's analysis of non-gateway messages are also happen to r e2e,i 's analysis. Furthermore, as the interference caused by dynamically arrived higher priority gateway messages is inter-dependent in two CAN, to define in what kind of situation they will cause the maximal interference on m i from the end-to-end's point of view is another challenge for r e2e,i 's analysis.

div.head: IV. INTERFERENCE ANALYSIS FOR GATEWAY MESSAGES
div.p: From the above analysis, we can find that the challenges for WCRT analysis of messages in gateway-interconnected CAN are all coming from the gateway messages. As a result, as the basis for message's WCRT analysis, we will focus on how to analyze the interference from gateway messages in this section. To make the description clear, we assume that m i is a non-gateway message, and the analysis object are dhp GW (i) messages, m k ∈ dhp GW (i). As explained before, the arriving pattern of m k in m i 's CAN sou is dynamic, thus one classical approach is to treat it as a sporadic message and set the closest distance between the arriving time of two continuous instances in m i 's CAN sou as its period just like [4,5] did. By doing this, the dynamic arriving m k is transformed into a periodic message in m i 's CAN sou and we can reuse the existing method to analyze its interference. But this approach will bring much pessimism to the interference analysis of m k , as the response time of its instances is changeable from C k to r s,k , thus the variation range of the distance between the arriving time of two continuous instances is very large. We propose a new definition busy sequence to capture the characteristic of dynamic arriving m k , which can get a tighter bound of its interference.

div.head: Definition 1: Busy sequence (BS k ) of dhp GW (i) message m k The instance sequence that includes the maximal number of instances of m k that can finish its transmission in m i 's CAN des and arrive at m i 's CAN sou in any time period of t is defined as the busy sequence BS k of m k .
div.p: Fig. 3 describes the BS k of m k , which starts from T 0 . T 0 indicates the arriving time of the first instance of m k in m i 's CAN sou , which equals to the finishing time of it in m i 's CAN des . It shows that when the first instance is finished at its WCRT and the following other instances are finished as soon as they are arrived in m i 's CAN des , the number of arrived instances in m i 's CAN sou in any time period of t that starts from T 0 is maximized for m k . For BS k , only the distance between the arriving time of the first and the second instance is equal to the closest distance between the arriving time of two continuous instances in m i 's CAN sou : (T k -r s,k +C k ). The distance between the arriving time of any other two continuous instances of m k in m i 's CAN sou is constrained by its period in m i 's CAN des , thus it equals to T k . Consequently, compared with the sporadic message model used in [4,5], the definition of busy sequence can get a tighter bound of the interference that would be caused by m k . Equation 1shows how to calculate the number of arrived instances NUM k (t) for BS k during any time period of t that starts from T 0 . For periodically arriving messages such as shp(i) messages in m i 's CAN sou , their busy sequences are corresponding to the periodically arriving instance sequences.

div.p: However, the definition of busy sequence can only defines the maximal interference that would be caused by each dhp GW (i) message, how to define the total interference that would be caused by all dhp GW (i) messages is quite another matter. The direct and intuitive assumption is that all dhp GW (i) messages arrive at m i 's CAN sou at the same time, thus the total interference equals to the sum of interference that is caused by each dhp GW (i) message. But as CAN messages are scheduled non-preemptively, the arriving time in m i 's CAN sou is under distance constraint for different dhp GW (i) messages. Next, we give the Definition 2 to capture this fact. Definition 2: The minimum distance constraint (MDC k ) of dhp GW (i) message m k For dhp GW (i) message m k , before its arriving in m i 's CAN sou , there will be an interval where no other dhp GW (i) messages can arrive. The theoretical low bound of this interval is equals to its C k , thus we define C k as the minimum distance constraint MDC k of m k .

We only consider the MDC k for the first instance of dhp GW (i) messages, it is impossible to consider the MDC k for all instances of them considering their interleaving transmissions. In spite of this, the analyzed interference of each dhp GW (i) messages is still conservative as we assume that their instances arrive with the busy sequence pattern. Even under this assumption, there is already n! different scenarios if there are n dhp GW (i) messages. However, MDC k can only defines the relative distance relation between m k and the other dhp GW (i) messages, to get the upper bound of the total interference that would be caused by all dhp GW (i) messages, we need to define the absolute distance relation among them, which means that we need to define the arriving order of all dhp GW (i) messages in m i 's CAN sou . As a result, we need to search all possible arriving orders of dhp GW (i) messages, and the object is to find the arriving order that would cause the maximal interference to m i . To clarify the description, we use the ADC k to indicate the absolute distance constraint between m k and the first arrived dhp GW (i) messages.

During the searching process, we can only determine the ADC k for those messages with determined arriving order, the ADC k of the other messages not only depend on their own C k , but also on the arriving order of the messages with determined arriving order. Therefore, the ADC k of all dhp GW (i) messages can only be determined after the arriving order of all messages are decided, which means that the generation of all possible arriving orders of dhp GW (i) messages is a must to get the arriving order that would cause the maximal interference on m i . The proposed exhaustive searching algorithm that is based on the depth-first searching [8] and can generate all the possible arriving orders of dhp GW (i) messages is shown in Algorithm 1, and the complexity of it is O(n!).

div.p: Theorem 1: The total interference caused by all dhp GW (i) messages on m i can be upper bounded by ADC k correlated busy sequences of all dhp GW (i) messages. Proof: First, dhp GW (i) messages cannot arrive at m i 's CAN sou at the same time, the ADC k that is only considered for their first instances just captures this fact. Second, ADC k is defined based on C k of each dhp GW (i) message, and the corresponding searching algorithm is to find the arriving order of dhp GW (i) messages that would cause the maximal interference on m i . And after the arriving order of dhp GW (i) messages is determined, each dhp GW (i) message arrives with its busy sequence, thus it can upper bound its interference on m i . Consequently, the ADC k correlated busy sequences of all dhp GW (i) messages can upper bound their total interference on m i .

As the complexity of Algorithm 1 is O(n!), it cannot be used when the number of dhp GW (i) messages is big. Thus, we propose another simplified searching algorithm that is inspired from [9] to define the MDC k relation among dhp GW (i) messages. That is we only consider the MDC k between the first arrived dhp GW (i) message and all the other dhp GW (i) messages, and we ignore the MDC k for all the other dhp GW (i) messages. As this assumption can only bring more pessimism into the interference analysis of all dhp GW (i) messages, the analyzed WCRT of m i will still be safe. Complexity of this simplified ordering algorithm is O(n).

div.head: V. THE PROPOSED WCRT ANALYSIS METHOD
div.p: After the above analysis, we solved the challenge about how to define the interference for dynamic arriving gateway messages. To tackle the challenge about the interdependency between messages in two CAN, we propose the following general processes for message's WCRT analysis:
• First, sort all messages inside the whole system in order of decreasing priority;

• Second, analyze their WCRT according to the order of decreasing priority. If the current m i is a nongateway message, analyze its r s,i ; if the current message is a gateway message, analyze its r e2e,i . Since when we try to analyze the WCRT of m i , the WCRT of all the other messages with priority higher than m i in both two CAN are already analyzed. Therefore, all kinds of interference that would happen to m i can be determined. Next, we will show how to analyze the r s,i and r e2e,i in detail.

div.head: A. The WCRT Analysis for Non-Gateway Messages
div.p: The definition of the busy period is fundamental to the WCRT analysis, for r s,i 's analysis of non-gateway message m i , the level-i busy period is defined similarly with [6] as follows: Definition 3: The level-i busy period of m i

• It starts at some time t s when a message with priority i or higher is queued ready to be transmitted, and no messages with priority i or higher waiting for transmission were queued strictly before t s ;

div.head: • It is a contiguous period of time during which no message with priority lower than i can win arbitration and start transmission; • It ends at the earliest time t e when the bus becomes idle, ready for the next round of arbitration and
div.p: transmission, yet no messages with priority i or higher waiting for transmission were queued strictly before t e . This time interval [t s , t e ) is the level-i busy period of m i , and r s,i is corresponding to the maximal level-i busy period w s,i that begins with the so called critical instant [10].

div.head: Definition 4: The critical instant for r s,i 's analysis of m i
div.p: • The arriving time of m i is synchronized with each shp(i) message; • The arriving time of m i is synchronized with the dhp GW (i) message set; • m i experiences the maximal blocking time from B s,i , where B s,i =max(C i , C m , C l ), m∈ slp(i), l∈ dlp GW (i). Theorem 2: When m i meets the critical instant conditions, the corresponding level-i busy period will be the maximal.

Proof: According to the sufficient schedulability test condition proposed for one single CAN [6], when m i experiences the maximal blocking from B s,i , and the arriving of m i is synchronized with all the other messages with higher priority than m i (they are represented as shp(i) in this paper), the level-i busy period will be the maximal. Based on given interference analysis in section III, we can easily extend this sufficient test condition to the gateway-interconnected CAN, where the interference caused by dhp GW (i) messages needs to be included in the level-i busy period and B s,i also needs to be extended to include the dlp GW (i) messages. As dhp GW (i) messages are asynchronous with m i , thus when it also synchronized with the arriving of m i , the level-i busy period of m i will be the maximal w s,i . According to the Theorem 1, the synchronization between m i and the dhp GW (i) message set means m i is synchronized with the first arrived dhp GW (i) message. Inside the w s,i , all messages with priority higher than m i such as shp(i) and dhp GW (i) messages will arrive with their busy sequence pattern. Thus, according to the definition of the critical instant, the maximal level-i busy period w s,i can be analyzed iteratively as follows:

div.head: B. The WCRT Analysis for Gateway Messages
div.p: Considering the intractability for r e2e,i 's analysis as analyzed in section III, we take a division approach by ignoring the inter-dependency between interference in two CAN that is caused by higher priority gateway messages, where the r e2e,i is divided into two separate parts as shown in Fig. 6. The first part represents the WCRT of m i in its CAN sou , as it indicates the same meaning as r s,i of nongateway messages, we also denote it as r s,i ; the second part represents the WCRT of m i in its CAN des and we denote it as r d,i . As we ignore the processing time inside the gateway for gateway messages, r e2e,i of m i can be calculated as follows. For both r s,i and r d,i , they will correspond with a level-i busy period as shown in Fig. 6. In section V.A, we already explained how to analyze w s,i and r s,i , next we will explain about how to analyze w d,i and r d,i . Fig. 2(b) illustrates all kinds of interference that would happen to m i when m i in its CAN des . The interference pattern of shp GW (i) and dhp(i) messages for r d,i 's analysis is the same with that of dhp GW (i) and shp(i) messages for r s,i 's analysis, respectively. The only difference is that m i is a gateway message that belongs to the same CAN with shp GW (i) messages, thus there is also the MDC k between m i and all shp GW (i) messages. But for r s,i 's analysis, the MDC k only exists for dhp GW (i) messages. This difference add much complexity to the r d,i 's analysis, because when we try to define the interference that would be caused by all shp GW (i) messages, we need to decide the arriving order of both m i and shp GW (i) messages. And depending on the specific arriving order of m i , there will be several candidate positions for dhp(i) messages to start their interference. As a result, the critical instant of the maximal level-i busy period w d,i cannot be uniquely determined. Thus, the complexity for r d,i 's analysis of m i is increased to O(n*n!).

In this paper, we take a simplified but more pessimistic approach by ignoring the MDC k between m i and all shp GW (i) messages. Under this assumption, all kinds of interference are the same for the analysis of r d,i and r s,i as we described before, thus r d,i 's analysis is transformed into the same situation with that of the r s,i 's analysis. Consequently, we can reuse the analysis method proposed for r s,i 's analysis. The maximal level-i busy period w d,i of m i in its CAN des can be calculated as follows accordingly for each possible arriving order of shp GW (i) messages:

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS
div.p: In section V, we already proved that the proposed method is correct and can get the safe upper bound of WCRT for messages in gateway-interconnected CAN. Next, we will further show the effectiveness of the proposed method by comparing it with a full space searching based simulator. The simulator is implemented by searching all the possible execution scenarios, where both the message combination and the offset relation among messages are considered. As the complexity of the simulator grows exponentially, we use the small message set shown in Fig. 1 as the experimental I. In this experiment, both Algorithm 1 and the simplified searching algorithm are used to find the arriving order of the gateway messages that would cause the maximal interference on m i .

Table II shows the result about the small message set. As the result is the same for the Algorithm 1 based method and the simplified searching based method, we only show one of them. We can find that for both r s,i and r d,i , the analysis result is close to the simulator's result. But for r e2e,i , the pessimism is relatively bigger. The reason is that for r s,i 's and r d,i 's analysis, the main pessimism comes from the definition of the busy sequence. But for r e2e,i 's analysis, we took a division approach and ignored the inter-dependency between interference caused by higher priority gateway messages in two CAN, which brings another source of pessimism. For this message set, the simulator and the proposed method took about 4 minutes and less that 1 second to get the result, respectively.

Another big real message set provided by automobile manufacturer is used to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. It includes 65 messages that are assigned into 14 ECUs, we assume that CAN is with the bandwidth of 500 kbps, thus the bus load it about 53%. We randomly divided it into two sub systems and set 30% of the messages as gateway messages, and the bus loads for the two CAN are 41.58% and 37.16%, respectively. As the message set is big, both Algorithm 1 based method and the simulator cannot get the WCRT within a reasonable time, thus only the simplified searching based method is used to analyze the message's WCRT. It took less than 1 second to get the result and the detail is shown in Fig. 7, where WCRT-SRC represents the r s,i and WCRT-DES represents the r d,i , and the message with smaller number indicates the message with higher priority.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: The main contribution of this paper is a schedulability analysis method that tackled the presented challenges and can get the safe upper bound of WCRT for messages in gateway-interconnected CAN. The safety of the proposed method is proved, and by comparing it with a simulator and applying to a big real message set, its effectiveness is also demonstrated.

According to the analyzed result, the pessimism in the analyzed r e2e,i is relatively big, therefore we will try to reduce it in the future by trying to analyze it from the end-to-end's level of view.
